passage: In the week before bonfire night in Leeds, Nour started counting. Monday, a supply teacher: "Your English is very good!" Nour had been born two streets from the school. Tuesday, a boy in chemistry: "But where are you really from?" "Leeds." "No, like, really." Wednesday, a dinner lady asked if she was fasting, though it wasn't Ramadan. Thursday, a girl in drama called her "so articulate, for someone like you". None of them meant much by it. Each remark took about four seconds. By Friday, at the bonfire-night stall, Nour stood a little apart from the group, hood up, feeling like a guest in her own town. Her friend Tomas handed her a toffee apple. "You've gone quiet this week." "Just tired of being asked where I'm from," she said. "I'm from here."

qa.q: Where was Nour born?
qa.a: Two streets from the school.

qa.q: How did Nour feel by Friday at the bonfire-night stall?
qa.a: She felt singled out and tired, like a guest in her own town, after a week of small remarks.

qa.q: How could Tomas support Nour now?
qa.a: Tomas could listen without playing it down, accept that the small remarks add up, and back her up if someone asks again.

qa.q: Why might the people who made the remarks not see the harm?
qa.a: Each made only one quick comment and didn't mean much by it, so none of them saw the whole week of repetition that Nour carried.

grounding: A teenager hears small remarks about her English and origin all week, and the repetition leaves her feeling like an outsider in her own town.

passage: Last Holi our whole building played in the parking lot, and I thought I was being funny. Kunal from the fourth floor came out grinning, and I shouted, "Lucky you! With your dark skin the colour won't even show!" A few people laughed. I laughed too; I honestly thought it was a friendly joke, like teasing someone for being tall. Kunal's grin stayed, but he went home early. Two days later his sister stopped me by the lift. "Simran," she said, very calmly, "Kunal has heard jokes about his skin his whole life, from relatives, strangers, school. Yours was just the newest." My face burned. I kept saying, "But I didn't mean it like that." She said, "I know. It still landed like that." That evening I knocked on their door and said sorry to Kunal properly, without explaining myself.

qa.q: When did Kunal's sister stop Simran by the lift?
qa.a: Two days later.

qa.q: How did Simran feel when Kunal's sister explained?
qa.a: Simran felt shocked and ashamed, face burning, because a joke meant kindly had actually hurt.

qa.q: What did Simran get right in the end?
qa.a: Simran apologised to Kunal properly the same evening, without explaining or defending the intention.

qa.q: What might the joke have felt like for Kunal?
qa.a: It probably stung as one more in a lifetime of remarks about his skin, even though he kept grinning and just went home early.

grounding: A teenager makes a Holi joke about a neighbour's skin, sincerely thinking it friendly, and is shocked to learn it hurt.

passage:
Monday, the week before winter exams. In the library queue Kalyani laughs, "Tanuja, say 'hospital' again, it's so cute, so village!" Two others giggle. Tanuja smiles, says nothing, and her cheeks stay hot through the whole chapter she is meant to be reading.
Wednesday. In the shower, in the canteen, before sleep, Tanuja keeps replaying it. Is she overreacting? It was a joke. But it's the fourth one this month. Speaking up means awkwardness in their group right before exams. Staying quiet means carrying it. She is tired either way.
Saturday. On the walk back from the last paper, Tanuja says, lightly but clearly, "Kalyani, the village jokes about how I talk, I don't enjoy them." Kalyani blinks. "Oh. I thought you didn't mind." "I minded," Tanuja says. The rest of the walk is quiet, and oddly lighter.

qa.q: What word did Kalyani ask Tanuja to say again?
qa.a: Hospital.

qa.q: What is Tanuja worried about on Wednesday?
qa.a: She worries she is overreacting and feels anxious that speaking up will cause awkwardness before exams, yet she is tired of carrying it silently.

qa.q: Which choice did Tanuja make, and what made it work?
qa.a: She spoke up lightly but clearly after exams, naming only the jokes about how she talks, which kept it calm and specific.

qa.q: How does Kalyani seem to see the jokes before Saturday?
qa.a: Kalyani seems to see them as harmless fun, believing Tanuja didn't mind because she always smiled.

grounding: A young adult teased about her accent weighs whether speaking up is worth the friction and finds carrying it silently tiring.

subtype: Being told about an unintended slight [Actor]
passage: It was the night before the Diwali break, the hostel Wi-Fi had died, and six of them were crammed into the one room with a hotspot, racing to submit their project. When Nandita fixed the bug that had stumped everyone, Ujjwal clapped. "Wow, you code really well for a girl!" She gave a thin smile and went back to her screen. After the submission, on the stairs, Hrithik stopped him. "Hey. That line to Nandita. It sounded like girls usually can't." Ujjwal's first feeling was heat. "I was praising her! You're making me sound terrible." Hrithik just waited. Ujjwal stared at the steps. "Okay. How bad?" "She went quiet for an hour." The next morning Ujjwal found Nandita at the bus stand. "What I said last night came out wrong, and I'm sorry. You're just a good coder." She nodded. He didn't ask her to say it was fine.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal say to Nandita after she fixed the bug?
qa.a: "Wow, you code really well for a girl!"

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel when Hrithik first raised it?
qa.a: He felt defensive and embarrassed, heat rising, as if he had been misjudged when he meant to praise her.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal get right the next morning?
qa.a: He apologised for how it landed, restated the praise without the qualifier, and didn't ask Nandita to reassure him.

qa.q: What might the remark have been like for Nandita?
qa.a: It likely stung, turning a proud moment into a reminder that some people expect girls to be worse, so she went quiet for an hour.

grounding: A student quietly told that his compliment to a classmate landed badly feels defensive, then listens, apologises for the effect and asks for no comfort.

passage:
Subject: A small thing from today's meeting
Hi Harish,
Thanks for pushing the vendor deal through today; your numbers were solid.
One small thing, and I'm raising it because I think you'd want to know. When you said, "Irawati, you'll take notes, na? You're good at that," I know you meant it kindly. But it's the fourth meeting in a row where I've been asked to take notes or order lunch while the analysis goes to someone else. It's started to feel like that's where I get placed.
I might be missing something; maybe there's a reason I'm not seeing? If so, tell me. If not, could we rotate note-taking from next week? I'd also like to present the pricing slide on Monday.
Happy to talk over tea.
Irawati

qa.q: How many meetings in a row has Irawati been asked to take notes or order lunch?
qa.a: It is the fourth meeting in a row.

qa.q: How does Irawati seem to feel about being asked to take notes again?
qa.a: Irawati seems frustrated and a little hurt at being placed in note-taking again and again, yet calm enough to assume Harish meant well.

qa.q: What makes Irawati's email likely to keep the relationship intact?
qa.a: It opens with real thanks, says the remark was meant kindly, asks if there is a reason, and offers a concrete fix: rotating notes and presenting the pricing slide.

qa.q: How might Harish react on reading the email?
qa.a: Harish may feel surprised and a bit embarrassed at first, but the kind tone and the offer of tea make it easier to see the pattern without feeling attacked.

grounding: A young professional tells a colleague calmly that a well-meant remark fits a pattern, asks what was meant and proposes a fix.

passage:
"Oi, Tarun! Nice voice. Sing for us, na!" Mohit squeaked in a high pitch, and his table laughed.
Tarun kept his eyes on his rajma rice.
Yogesh picked up his tray and walked over. "This seat free?"
Tarun looked up, surprised. "Uh. Yeah."
Yogesh sat. "Did you finish the physics worksheet? Question six is killing me."
"Six? You have to use the second formula."
"Show me after lunch?"
"Okay."
From the other table: "Yogesh, you joined the choir too?"
Yogesh didn't turn around. "Question six, Tarun. The second formula how?"
The laughter thinned out. Mohit's table got busy with their own food.
When the bell rang, the two of them walked out together, still arguing about the formula.

qa.q: What was Tarun eating?
qa.a: Rajma rice.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh ask about question six instead of scolding Mohit?
qa.a: Yogesh seems uneasy watching the mocking but wants to support Tarun calmly, so ordinary talk shows Tarun he isn't alone without starting a fight.

qa.q: What worked about Yogesh's approach?
qa.a: Sitting with Tarun, ignoring the jibe and walking out with him lowered the temperature and left the mockers without an audience.

qa.q: What might it mean to Tarun that Yogesh sat down?
qa.a: It likely made Tarun feel relieved and less alone, turning a humiliating lunch into an ordinary chat about physics.

grounding: A student sees a classmate mocked in the canteen and quietly sits and walks out with him instead of lecturing the mocker.

passage: The college bus was forty minutes late, stuck behind a waterlogged underpass, and everyone was short-tempered. In the back row, two seniors grabbed Eshaan's phone again, typed something from his account and tossed it back, laughing. The third time that week. Mridul, wedged by the door, felt his anger rise and started toward them. Then he stopped. Would a scene on a stuck bus help Eshaan, or just make him the centre of it? At the college gate, away from the crowd, he caught up. "I saw the phone thing. What do you want? I can go with you to the anti-ragging cell, or talk to them, or just sit next to you on the bus. Your call." Eshaan looked at his shoes. "Come with me to the cell? Now, before I lose my nerve." They went. The teacher on duty wrote down both seniors' names, asked Eshaan for screenshots, and called the seniors in that afternoon.

qa.q: How late was the college bus?
qa.a: Forty minutes late.

qa.q: Why did Mridul stop himself from confronting the seniors on the bus?
qa.a: He felt angry but also unsure, worried a scene would only make Eshaan the centre of attention rather than help him.

qa.q: What made Mridul's help respectful?
qa.a: He asked Eshaan privately what he wanted and offered choices, then followed his lead to the anti-ragging cell.

qa.q: How might Eshaan feel being told "Your call"?
qa.a: Eshaan likely feels respected and less powerless, able to choose the help he wants after days of having control taken from him.

grounding: A student who sees a peer harassed asks him privately what help he wants instead of taking over, and follows his lead to report it.

passage: Under the cherry blossoms in a Kyoto park, the hanami picnic was going well until a man on the next mat, red-faced from sake, muttered that foreigners should go home, looking straight at Valentina. She had already decided to ignore him. Then Hiroshi was on his feet. He told the man off in a loud voice for two full minutes, turned to the other mats and announced that he, personally, had always fought against this kind of thing, and that Valentina was "very upset". She wasn't, not until then. Everyone was looking at her. "Thank you," she said later, and meant it. But on the train home she felt small, as if she had become a story about Hiroshi's courage. What she had wanted was simple: someone to ask, quietly, "Want to move mats?"

qa.q: Where was the hanami picnic?
qa.a: Under the cherry blossoms in a Kyoto park.

qa.q: How did Valentina feel on the train home?
qa.a: She felt grateful to Hiroshi but also small, as if the moment had turned into a story about his courage.

qa.q: What could Hiroshi try next time?
qa.a: He could quietly ask Valentina what she wants, like whether to move mats, and follow her lead instead of speaking for her.

qa.q: How might Hiroshi see his own actions?
qa.a: Hiroshi probably believes he was brave and supportive, without noticing that he made a scene and spoke for Valentina.

grounding: A young woman targeted by a stranger's remark is defended loudly by a friend who speaks for her, and feels grateful yet smaller.

passage:
Supervisor's note: team conduct, week 12
I am recording this because it matters. On Tuesday, at the chai counter, one of the analysts joked about Deepa's hearing aid, cupping a hand to his ear and shouting "WHAT?" while she was out on a client visit. A few people laughed. Vaibhav didn't. He said calmly, "Not funny. She's not here to answer, and she's better at this job than most of us." The laughter stopped. Then on Thursday, in the planning meeting, when the client dashboard idea came up as if it were new, Vaibhav said, "That's Deepa's design from last month. Let's make sure it's credited to her." I have spoken privately to the analyst who made the joke. I am also noting Vaibhav's conduct for his review and have asked him to help with next month's inclusion session.
Hansa, team supervisor

qa.a: She was out on a client visit.

qa.q: Why might Vaibhav have spoken up at the chai counter?
qa.a: He likely felt uncomfortable and protective, unwilling to let a colleague be mocked when she wasn't there to answer.

qa.q: What did Hansa do next, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: Hansa spoke privately to the analyst, noted Vaibhav's conduct for his review and asked him to help with the inclusion session, backing small, consistent acts.

qa.q: How might Deepa feel if she learned about Thursday's meeting?
qa.a: Deepa would likely feel respected and valued, knowing her design was credited even when she wasn't in the room.

grounding: A colleague calmly challenges a joke about an absent co-worker's hearing aid and later makes sure her idea is credited in a meeting.

passage: In March, Javier posted a photo of the office iftar in Madrid with the caption: "Proud to work somewhere that celebrates everyone!" It got two hundred likes. He liked that. The next week, Siddiq asked quietly whether the Thursday team lunch meeting could move to the morning for the rest of Ramadan, since three of them were fasting. Javier frowned. The lunch was his favourite part of the week, and the restaurant was booked. "Can't you just sit with us and not eat? It's only a month." Siddiq said, "I could. But you posted about celebrating everyone." Javier felt heat in his face. "That's not fair. I've been really supportive." Siddiq shrugged and went back to his desk. Javier opened his phone, looked at the two hundred likes, and for the first time they felt a little empty.

qa.q: How many likes did Javier's post get?
qa.a: Two hundred.

qa.q: How did Javier feel when Siddiq mentioned the post?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and defensive, his face hot, insisting he had been supportive instead of listening.

qa.q: What would real support from Javier look like now?
qa.a: Listening to Siddiq, moving the meeting to the morning for Ramadan even though it costs him the lunch, and accepting the correction without sulking.

qa.q: What might Siddiq have felt when Javier said "It's only a month"?
qa.a: Siddiq probably felt let down and unheard, since the public support disappeared as soon as it cost Javier something.

grounding: A young professional posts public support mainly to look good and loses interest when a colleague asks for something that costs him.
